utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I received no information about preliminaries to deal with first. Therefore, is the Stanisic Defence ready to call its expert witness, Mr. Browne?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could Mr. Browne be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Jordash, needless to say, that you asked for two hours of examination-in-chief, that the Chamber has read the report for Mr. Browne; it had ample opportunity to do so over the many, many weeks. There's no need to repeat anything in there. And I hope Mr. Browne is aware that he's not appearing before a jury but before a professional Bench which has read in detail the report he prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that's clear to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I don't have to remind him, most likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Browne.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text has been handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Browne. Please be seated. Mr. Browne, for your information, the Chamber has read your report very carefully, so there's no need to repeat whatever is in the report. You'll first be examined by Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Browne. Could you give your full name and date of birth for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I am David Richard Browne, and my date of birth is 24/2/49.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, 1D05300, which is a copy of your report which His Honour has just referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number; it was not shown on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. 1D05300.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Whilst the report is coming onto the screen, let's deal, if I can -- oh, there it is. Let's deal very quickly with your qualifications. Between 1974 and 1983 you were employed as a forgery officer in the -- in Her Majesty's immigration service in the UK. What did that, in very brief, involve?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I examined -- I was based at ports, airports, by and large, and it was my job to examine passports that were encountered, either carried by passengers, used by passengers, or in bags, and other documents as well. And I had to examine for evidence of fraud and report my findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were you using equipment or just your naked eye?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Oh, no, we had specialist equipment at port level. Later on, more advanced equipment was made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In 1983 you were appointed the senior document examiner in the national forgery intelligence section of the immigration service. What did that involve?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Well, it was -- I was one of the two main expert witnesses for the immigration service at that time to give evidence in courts. We had, in the national forgery intelligence section, a great deal more -- more advanced equipment, and we used that to decide whether documents were forged. We worked not only for immigration officers at the ports, but we worked for immigration officers all over the country, and we also worked for the police and patrons customs and excise and inland revenue and other government agencies. And then it was my -- one of my main tasks was to go to court and give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What kind of documents were you looking at?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Passports, driving licences, study documents, certificates of education, and things of that nature. In the case of when we're dealing with police forces and so on and so forth, we had to examine believed-to-be counterfeit documents and then assist the police with raids on print shops and forgery factories to see if those forged documents had come from those forgery factories. And we had to basically examine every document that was brought in, and it could be visas, it could be passports, it could be diaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what kind of skills or equipment were employed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Well, basically, it's true to say, the most important equipment are the eyes. We have to examine a document for any evidence that we can find, and the first examination is always of a straight forward visual one. We use microscopes, low-powered microscopy, by and large. And then we have to go into further detail. We have to look in the infrared and ultraviolet to see if there's any evidence of forgery or fraud. Infrared light enables us to separate one ink from another because of the chemical compensation of the inks. Ultraviolet light enables us to identify areas of a particular page that may have been altered by chemical means. And also, because of security printing, most of which is ultraviolet-sensitive, if any of the printing has been removed by mechanical means, then the ultraviolet light will show that. The other useful aspect of ultraviolet light is it enables us to separate one type of paper from another because of the -- ordinary paper, that is, because of the way paper is made, the chemical compensation changes from making to making.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then you left the immigration service in 1994 to join network forensic services as the resident document examiner?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: In ninety -- in early 1994, yes. I came out into, as it were, private practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what kind of work were you doing there precisely?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Well, the same, except the shift -- there was a shift in the emphasis of our work; whereas before, in government service, 99 per cent of my work was for prosecution services. After I left, then, there was a shift in the emphasis; some of it was for prosecution, some of it was for defence. And also civil cases. It didn't make any difference to me who instruct me. The report still has to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what kind of documents were you examining?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Then I was examining a wider range of documents. I was examining contracts of employment. I was examining wills and things of that nature which I wouldn't normally have seen when I was in government service.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then in December 1997 you left network to found the independent company Berkley Security Bureau Forensic Limited?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes. And since then, we've now been taken over by a company called Diligence. So it's Diligence BSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what kind I've work have you been doing with this company?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: All the same. I'm employed as an expert in document examination and reporting, so it's the same work. And I still examine passports and driving licences and documents of identity, and I still examine contracts and other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you present that evidence in reports or court? How --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Report first. And if required, then court. Everything we have to do, we have to do with the possibility that we may be called to court to explain what we have examined and what we have written about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just have a moment, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when you were asked, as we can see, if we move up the page on the screen to your instructions, you were instructed by myself of the Stanisic Defence team to examine these notebooks/diaries. Was this a request which was consistent with the type of work you'd been doing, or different, or how would you categorise it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I have done examinations of this nature before. Until we see the book, we don't know if there's anything wrong. We don't know if pages have been changed, but I have seen books in the past where pages have been taken out and new ones put in. It's a very common way of forging passports, substituting pages. There's no difference whether it's a security document, as a passport, or whether it's an ordinary handwritten notebook or diary. In big corporate cases, even in this electronic age, a lot of people write things down. And later sometimes even lawyers have been moved to alter the records in their case files to avoid censure and criticism. And I have been involved in examining such case files in the past. I mean, there's no real difference between this and other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What were your precise instructions here, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I was to examine the books, the way the books have been put together. I wasn't instructed to take any -- to undertake any examination of the handwriting. I couldn't, anyway. I don't speak Serbian, and I have no knowledge of handwritten Cyrillic script. That matter, as I understand it, as part of my instructions, has already been dealt with by another expert who does do all of that. I was examined -- expected to examine the -- the books and to see if there's any evidence that there may have been any tampering of the books. I was to look for anomalies, basically, and then to report the findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you were given - I don't think there's any dispute here - you were given and shown a number of documents, including the notebooks themselves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I was first shown print-outs -- sorry, scanned copies of pages of the notebooks. I was allowed to examine a number of notebooks in a preliminary case viewing, as it were. And in November last year I was allowed access to all of the notebooks under certain preconditions, which was fair enough. And, yes, I was given access to all of the books.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, 1D05472, which is the examination protocol that was agreed between the Prosecution and Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Jordash. Your previous question seems to distinguish between the books and other documents. You said: "You were given and shown a number of documents, including the notebooks themselves." Which remains another category on which the witness has not said anything. And although we find references in his report now and then to documents unknown to this Chamber -- often unknown to this Chamber and not further specified in the report, I wonder whether we should not know in more detail what documentary material, apart from the notebooks, has been made available to the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. I was going to return to that issue, but I'll deal with it straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been preferable to have in the report, but you'll understand that it's easier to prepare if you have that information readily available. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, 1D03490.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you shown a number of documents which recorded in one form or another the way in which the search and seizure of these documents had taken place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Sorry. I -- I -- the reason, Your Honour, for the -- my confusing answer - I beg your pardon - I was served with a great many documents, copied into a great many documents, which were copy documents. I wasn't required to examine them per se. They were just provided for background information. I apologise for not making that clearer in my reply earlier. I was provided with copies of a large number of documents, some of it in what I presume to be Serbian, and others in English. And there were photographs and lists of exhibits, but I didn't have to examine those. If you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but if I -- if you allow me to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A, I would say methodological requirement is that if someone has to read a report, irrespective of whether you examined those other reports, they may have had an influence on your conclusions. And then, of course, it's of primary importance that the reader of the reporter knows exactly what the content of that material is, whether you examined it or not, and that is the reason why I raised it, this matter. That for full transparency and for a full opportunity to follow your line of reasoning, it's essential to know exactly what was available to you at that time. Including the content of that material. And that does not appear in the report apart from some references here and there. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash. I would not have addressed the expert, but since he started explaining on the basis of a matter I raised with you, I thought it would be appropriate to briefly respond to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me try to do this shortly, because I don't think there's going to be any dispute on these issues. This is the front sheet of a particular document which I think you've seen, is that right, in preparation for your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we move to page 17 in e-court to a statement by the head of the service, Police Advisor Dejan Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you shown this letter?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: A letter by a police officer from the Serbian Ministry of Interior detailing the way in which the document - the particular notebooks which were recovered in 2010 - how they were, in fact, found; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: That is what the document seems to say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we go to page 18. This perhaps is the critical aspect for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you informed through this document where the notebooks were allegedly found during the Serbian Ministry of Interior's search? And particularly, looking at paragraph 3, where it notes: "The notebooks purportedly belonging to Ratko Mladic were also found at two locations: Some of them in Bosiljka Mladic's bedroom, in the space between two sections of the wardrobe placed on the other side of the bed opposite the chest of drawers where audiotapes were found; the others were found in the attack, which is accessed through opening in the bathroom ceiling."

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was this the sum-total of what you were told in relation or what the documents said in relation to the precise location where these notebooks were allegedly found?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Well, this is the writing. There are, I believe, a number of photographs referred to. And I had access to copies of those photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to the photographs, then, now, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Pardon, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps the best way to do this. Perhaps could I have moment, please. Okay. Let's do it this way. Please could we have on the screen 1D03486.1. 1D03486.1, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was this one of the photographs you were shown of a cabinet?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Is this the picture? All right. Yes, I've seen this photograph before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we can go to page 5, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 47.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Forty-eight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Forty-nine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Fifty-one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- these are a selection of some of the notebooks; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And 53.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Am I correct that you haven't seen and, as far as we're aware, there are no photographs of the books where they were allegedly found in the attic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: There are no photographs as far as I can make out. I haven't seen any photographs of the books in situ.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And for Your Honours' information: None, as far as we're aware, exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the same goes for the place between the two sections of the wardrobe where the books were allegedly found; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Not in situ or of any two wardrobes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Going back to page 51, the small selection of the notebooks which were photographed on the floor somewhere. Did you make any observations containing those books during your preparation of the report?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: The books are very clean. They are in an area which I can't identify where it is, what it is. They're on the floor. There's a great deal of dust and dirt around that area. There doesn't seem to be any dust and dirt on the books themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps we can also now turn to 1D03488.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Whilst that's coming onto screen: Did you read anything in the documentation provided by the Serbian Ministry of Interior or the Prosecution at the ICTY which stated or described who found the documents in the attic or who found the documents between the wardrobe? Were you assisted with that type of information? And if -- if -- well, would you answer that first. Were you assisted by that information?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: No. That information was not forthcoming. I didn't read any witness statement, as I would understand it, involving the recovery of the books.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you say as you would understand it, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: A witness statement, as I would understand it, is a statement made by an officer involved in any raid or of that nature. It basically says, I -- I was at a certain place, I did certain things, I found certain things, I took possession of those things, I was with this officer and that officer. I have not read any witness statement that says, I turned up at the door of that flat and I went inside and I found behind a panel, in a panel, upsidedown, between two wardrobes, I saw a pile of books. I have not read a statement from anybody who took the photographs. Neither have I seen a statement that introduces those photographs, the photographs I have seen, in evidence. So I have no idea, really, where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you shown this declaration by Tom Blaszczyk in the -- for the preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure I've seen that one before. It's a declaration. I'm not sure when it was dated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we can -- well, I can deal with this shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's dead the 30th of July, 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We're going to ask for these statements to be tendered, Your Honour, in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you told, therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we can go up in the two paragraphs so we can see paragraph 3 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you told, therefore, that the apartment where these notebooks were allegedly found had been searched previously in 2008?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes. I seem to remember mention that the apartment had been searched a number of times. But I don't know where I got that information from, to be fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But you had that information --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes. At some stage. I mean, it had no impact on my examination, of course, but it pans into place in due course. And I was aware that books had been seized in 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But you were not provided with any information concerning how those early searches or search had managed to miss these -- [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Not by -- not by whom, how they were found, where they were precisely found, the December 2008 books, I mean. I -- and of course I can't answer anything about why other books weren't found.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And perhaps it's obvious, but it's right, isn't it, you were not given, because as far as we're aware none exist, any photographs or records and the like relating to who precisely and where the 2008 books were found, the books that were recovered in 2008?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I was not provided with any such material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The type of statement that you've referred to a moment ago in relation to the --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- 2010. In relation to other items that were found during the search, were you shown a list of items besides these notebooks which were also allegedly found during that search?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we could turn, please, to 1D03463.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is this a document which you were shown during the preparation of your report, dealing with the -- some of the further details of the search, including the timing of the search there, at 7.49, completed at 2.00. Were you shown this statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I've seen that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we go over the page there, were you shown this aspect of the statement where, three quarters of the way down the page, the Serbian Ministry of Interior purportedly checking a computer at the site and sim cards and concluding at that time that they were of no relevance to their investigation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen that report before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's return to the report itself. I think that deals with the background. Well, last thing in relation to that: Were you shown also a photograph of a satellite phone found at the premises?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I think there are two photographs covering that particular item. One is the -- the outer casing of the phone, and the other is with the phone opened, or placing opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We'll return to that in a minute. Let's return to your report, 1D05300. You've referred a number of times to -- throughout the report, to ESDA, an electrostatic method of detecting indented impressions.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you just briefly describe what that was, or is.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Your Honour -- excuse me. Your Honour, ESDA is the electrostatic detection apparatus. It is a piece of technical equipment used in document laboratories all over the world, and it is a means of, without damaging a page, detecting any indented writing from documents that were above the page at the time they were written. And it enables us to make a permanent record of what those indentations are and what they look like for future use. But, as I say, the document itself, the page itself we're examining, is not damaged in the proceedings. And that was the whole idea of the equipment. It was designed in the 1970s, and essentially it hasn't changed in method or, indeed, success. It's a very useful tool. It enables us to establish on any piece of paper if anybody has been writing on top. There are certain technical occasions why such indentations may not show; for instance, pencil is not -- it just doesn't render itself terribly well to ESDA. It's all about pen pressure, and therefore fountain pens also tend not to leave many indentations, because obviously a fountain pen you don't need to press very hard to make a mark. But ball-point pens, fibre-point pens, and the like, the writing will come through on the page beneath. I've used it several times -- well, thousands of times, frankly, to see if the page I'm looking at has been under another page while it has been written.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would it have been useful in relation to this report?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Almost certainly. But the examination of books - to be fair, bound books - in using ESDA is not as simple as the majority of ESDA work. We have to separate one page from the book. We don't have to take it out, but we do have to manipulate the book in such a way so that we can place that page, and only that page, on the ESDA machine. And thereafter we can go through the normal ESDA procedure. For instance, I mean, I've examined pages in passports exactly like that. And it just requires more care and it requires a great deal of -- well, frankly, practice, but also we just -- we just have to be careful. And normally two people have to be involved to make sure that the book is not harmed in any way and everything is left intact at the end of the examination. The ESDA lift, which is the end result, is the permanent record of the indentations. But they're not -- they don't damage the document itself, and the document can then go back to doing whatever it was doing before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you didn't use ESDA for these -- or for this examination?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, that seems to be pretty clear from the report, isn't it? I mean, I find on over -- almost every page "no ESDA," "no ESDA," "no ESDA." So therefore, I would be surprised by any other answer than, of course, ESDA was not available to examine these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I was about to lead into the next part, which was why was that. It was just an introduction to ... but I'll put it more shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You didn't use ESDA because you were not permitted to; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes. ESDA was strictly forbidden under the terms of the examination protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would ESDA in your view have destroyed the books or damaged the books?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Used with care, I wouldn't have expected it to do so. But that's -- it's a dead issue, frankly, now. It would have helped.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move swiftly through your report, because it's quite self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash -- yes, now I've found it. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Twenty-two and 24, you would - again, I'm just picking out paragraphs to contrast with paragraph 30 - you talk about missing pages, but make no mention of indentations. How confident are you that you picked up indentations without the use of ESDA?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Well, as I think the protocol lays out, Your Honour, the equipment that the National Forensic Institute provided was state-of-the-art, very high quality equipment in the terms of the VSC that they made available to me throughout my examination. And that had the capability of directing light obliquely across a page to see -- which enables us to a certain extent to show up any indentations. The problem is, of course, that the pages are in the middle of a book and all -- there is writing all around that page, and those pages. So, whereas we can pick up indentations, matching the indentations to the pages before or after is because it is not as precise as ESDA, which gives you an absolute shot at the indented impressions. Matching them with the writing on the other side is less simple. In some cases we were able to prove the point that the indentations we think we can see seem to come from the writing on a page that's already still in the book, but in other cases we can -- we could not be a hundred per cent satisfied that we had actually picked up all indentation or been able to separate one indentation from the writing on either side. What ESDA does is show all the indentations, and we can then place that lift over pages that are still in the book and see if they match. And if they match, then that's the question answered. If they do not match, then there are indentations that have come -- that have gone missing from somewhere. So ESDA would have helped, but we cannot - and I'm sure the NFI scientists' exactly the same - we would not be able to say confidently that we'd picked up all the indentations using the oblique light.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we move to paragraph 54 of your report. And I think it's fair to say that this aspect of the report concerns a book where you found the most anomalies --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- or problems.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you say, at 55, a major difference lies in the state of the book. There are 28 pages that are loose. In fact, they are barely attached at all. And so on.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And at paragraph 56 you talk about inks that have been used then abandoned then picked up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps if I can hand out at this stage copies of part of that book so that this can be properly explained to the Chamber. Just one of the books.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I meanwhile, when this material is distributed, ask one additional question. I think you earlier said that if you can pick up indentation that you sometimes were but sometimes were not able to match those indentations with text written on one of the other pages, if I understood you well. Could you indicate where in the report we find such, if I could say, positive matches, where you said -- well, often the report says, Without ESDA we couldn't establish anything at all - where you found indentations which you could match to the text written on the adjacent, may I take it, the page which was above, the page on which you found the indentations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I will try and do that, Your Honour. Your Honour, if I can draw your attention to paragraph 35, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thirty-five.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if that answers -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, well, that's -- that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to some extent. To some extent also not. Because you say oblique light shows indentations that may have come from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 2236. It doesn't say that you found positive indications. And I'm now going back to your testimony that sometimes you were able to match, sometimes you're not able to match. It doesn't explain why, where you say it may have come from, whether there was any positive --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- indication established, because the report doesn't say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't possible to make an absolute -- enable us to make an absolute statement as to the origins of indentations. At page 31 -- at paragraph 31 - I beg your pardon, Your Honour - immediately above that, I cannot exclude the possibility that the missing page was torn out before the writing was made, but I'm unable to establish this one way or the other. If you like -- I mean, it is worthy because we're looking for anomalies. I'm looking for anomalies as per my instructions. And if I have found indications of the origin of the indentations within the book, then it ceases to be an anomaly. I can't make it certain -- we can't make it certain in those circumstances. So, yeah, it may have come from there, therefore that's -- it has to be good enough for me. I can't establish it without using ESDA, and therefore that's as good as it's going to get, Your Honour. But it doesn't become an issue for me once I think I've found an indication. I have to put it away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm especially focussing on your testimony where you said that in some cases -- the transcript is not very precise. I think, Mr. Jordash, I'm referring to page 18, line 19: "In some cases ... to come from the writing on the page that's already still in the book, but in other cases we can -- we could not be a hundred per cent satisfied that we had actually picked up all indentation or been able to separate one indentation from the writing on the other [sic] side." So it looks as if a distinction is made between positive matches you could establish and other situations where you were, as you said, at least not for a hundred per cent sure. And I'm looking now for the positive matches described in your report, and the examples you've given are mainly in the category of, it may have been without a clear positive match being established.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That, I'm afraid, Your Honour, is as good as it's going to get throughout because I would consider only ESDA is going to be absolutely positive. If we're looking at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- infrared oblique light, I'm not going to be able to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm fully happy with -- that's what I thought from the report. Therefore, I was a bit surprised by the testimony I just referred to a second ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, may I -- is it the word "positive" that you -- that hits you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's about matching the indentations to the pages before or after it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At -- and, Mr. Jordash, please assist me - where I read "at -- in case seem to come from the writing on the page that's already still in the book," which seems to -- a kind of positive match that you had reasons to believe that the indentations came from other writing in the book. And, as you said, "but in other cases we could not be a hundred per cent satisfied that we had actually picked up all the indentation or been able to separate one indentation from the writing on the other [sic] side." So there are apparently uncertain. And I do understand that the uncertainty goes, as a matter of fact, for all of the material.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does go in all of the indented impression business it is not certain. But if we found something that was a positive match -- not a precise match, but gives us indication that that's where it comes from, I've put that aspect to bed, as it were. It can't be raised any more, because we've got something that indicates that it may not be anomalous, the missing page. It's really not what's in the book at the moment; it's the missing page. Was the page torn out with writing on it? In which case I would expect to see indentations on either side. Or was the page -- the missing page taken out before there was any writing in existence? And that's as far as I can go. That's why I'm looking for the indentations on either side of the torn out page, to see if there's anything there that can't be linked to the pages on either side, existing writing in the book. But I can't be certain. When I'm saying "positive," I mean it sort of -- there are matches. That's not exactly a positive opinion or a certain opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We are about to look at these -- I don't know if you've been given a copy of that, of a colour copy of book 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And for Your Honours' information: This book contains P2531, pages 19 to 29; P2532, page 33 to 62; P2533, 76 to 81; and P2534, 115 to 116.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you, perhaps, find the page where -- which illustrates paragraph 56 of your report. Inks that had been used briefly, then abandoned, then picked up again later.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Bottom of page 4223. I'm using the J-0 number at the top, the red number. If we go down to page 7 in one ink, and indeed that has come from the page before as well, that ink, and then paragraph 8 and 9 are written in a different ink. And over the page we come to paragraph 10, which is written in the ink that was there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if I am -- for the record: What are we looking at exact -- I found it in my hard copy, so there's no problem with that, but for those who have to reconstruct later what we looked at, what the witness now explains is found in any document which is in evidence or is not in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This isn't in evidence -- [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it in evidence. So you're going to tender the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This -- this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- this document at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be wise to already assign a number, to save those, while reading the transcript at a later stage, to not know for pages and pages in what document they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. This is not the totality of book 16, I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but this is an -- this is a copied excerpt of certain pages of book 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. They are 4209 -- this is what Mr. Browne included in his report, 42 -- well, slightly -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it numbered throughout? Because then we find, in red, J00004209 [sic] on that cover page, which bears a large number 44. And is it then subsequently numbered until the last page, which is J000-4264?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It is. And I spoke out of turn. This is, in fact, the full book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is the full book.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At paragraph 54, Mr. Browne talks of an excerpt of the book. But this is the full book, which we would like to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You would like to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- tender that. Mr. Groome, any objections against -- because I'm afraid that those reading the transcript at later stages are lost without a clear reference to what we are looking at at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- Mr. Browne has just said earlier, or caught it, but he said, No, it's not. This is not the entire book.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Browne --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's -- agrees with my understanding of what we have before it us. Perhaps we could clarify that. And if we're going to tender the whole book, perhaps we can -- make sure that we in fact do have the entire book.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I think that I spoke correctly the first time and I think we're all in agreement this is not the full book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is it excerpts? Because I see that handwritten numbering at the top of the page starts at 1 and goes until 52. Does that mean that there are other pages which will follow, or is there an interruption halfway? I have not checked that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might assist the Chamber. The entire book is uploaded in e-court under 65 ter 5892. Perhaps that's the copy that we could tender, and consider that the printed copy we have before us is a facsimile of what's in e-court. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that contains similar red numbers as we find it in the hard copy before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I haven't verified it right now, Your Honour, but my understanding is, my recollection is, that it in fact does. These are colour scans of the -- high-resolution colour scans of the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Jordash, what are your plans? To tender this as a separate document or to rely on book 16 as -- in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm happy to tender it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Simatovic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I think you made reference to 65 ter 5892 which, as Madam Registrar informs me, is P2532. But she has a slight suspicion that you may have wanted to refer to another document which is uploaded as 65 ter -- and, Madam Registrar, perhaps you could express your mind on it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 5606 bears document ID J004209, which you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 65 ter 5606 is our information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the book in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You tender it. Mr. Groome has no objection. Mr. -- the Simatovic Defence has no objection either. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We deal with it now, Mr. Jordash. If it is part of your bar table motion, I take it that you'll strike it from that at a later stage, if it is. If it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Although we want the Cyrillic in evidence but for the point of showing Your Honours the difference in use of ink, so it should be a separate document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But we are aware that it may play a role in your bar table motion as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It certainly does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the number of this document, perhaps you identify it very clearly for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for document 5606 will be 3109, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were there other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the -- let me see. Is this P or D? It's tendered by Mr. Jordash, now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's P3109.

utterances.text: Any problem with having it as a P document --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH

utterances.text: -- in evidence? P --

utterances.text: Well, I think, after all, it's more appropriate to make it -- Mr. Jordash, you're tendering it, therefore, I would prefer to assign a D number to it rather than a P number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Then document 5606, instead of 3109, will receive number D767, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D767 is admitted into evidence, and P3109 is vacated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just going back to your report. Unless you wanted to say something more about the ink, Mr. Browne.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: No, not particularly. That does it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At paragraph 55 of your report you comment about the loose pages totalling 28 and the fact that very little glue seems to have been used to hold that together, contrasted with the spine which showed a significant amount of glue was used in the book's manufacture.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you able to say anything about the glue itself? Were there any other indications which could assist the Court?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: No, not particularly. The -- this book is one of the few books in this whole set of books that has not been bound with sewing. And it's been -- it's basically perfect binding which is basically single pages blocked together. A layer of glue is run down one part of the spine, or the head - it depends what sort of book it is. And a cover around the whole of that is then glued to hold the pages together. The spine is actually -- the cover has come off of this book completely, the outer cover. It's an unusual type of diary anyway. It's the -- it has a nice fine leather outside cover. And inside, it's very like the sort of gifts that people can buy to hold people's passports. The leather covering is slipped the back cover of the passport in one, and you slip the front cover, and you open it up and you've got the passport contained in a leather folder. This is exactly the same. You've got the leather cover with slots to take in the outer card cover, and it is the outer card cover that is the real cover of the book, which is glue -- has all the pages glued into it. The problem I had - and it is a -- it is -- it is an anomaly that I have been unable to reconcile - is that the pages that are coming loose have very little glue holding them together at all, and yet there's plenty of glue still in the -- the actual cover. And that glue will have gone in in liquid form so that if the cover has come apart, it should actually have come apart with the glue in the cover cracked, because that is the way these -- these books are just -- transpire when they -- when do fall apart, and I would have expected to find more glue on the pages. We haven't got much glue. It is an anomaly. I have not been able to reconcile that anomaly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question in that respect. If a certain number of pages are glued together and thus form a kind of a book, if you separate one or two or five or ten or 20 pages of that, is there a possibility that part of the glue which was attached to the separate pages leaves those individuals pages? And perhaps that on one page you might find, if I could say, a stretch of glue which would have attached to some of the other pages which are now loose, and that, therefore, the picture of the intensity of the glue on the loose pages might be different depending on whether I am dealing with page 1 or 3 or 20 or 25 which has been taken out? You understand what I mean? That if the pages are still all together, then the glue will cover those pages; whereas, if you take them apart, it could be that the glue is unevenly distributed among the pages which are taken out. Is there any possibility that this could have happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think not, Your Honour, purely and simply because the whole of the cover has come off. So all the pages are -- are loose from the cover, and certainly they've been separated from their glue base, if you like. If, of course, that glue base is the glue base from which they are examined. If I can demonstrate, and it is really an off-the-cuff demonstration. This is a standard pad. It's perfect bound. The pages running right, just single pages, they're blocked together, and they're glued up at the top. They've got a bit of tape around. And that is the spine. These are very common. And if I want to remove a page, or in this case two. I've removed two pages. And I've left a gap in here. And you can still see the glue. By and large, they -- but because this is this sort of pad, it's not perforated but it has torn the paper. There is glue left here. If I were to remove the whole of the spine, tape, and break the spine from the book, I would then have all the pages more or less glued together. In this case what I have is, the spine has been removed, and I have very little glue left at all, and that is less usual because the cover is going to separate -- it should separate from the glue more quickly than the actual page book. I'm sorry if that doesn't answer the question, but that was by way of a sort of demonstration, but it may not have demonstrated properly. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not entirely. Is there any way to compare the composition of the glue, the little glue left on some of the pages, and the glue left on the intact part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be beyond my competence, but the NFI, I'm sure, would be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there are perhaps possibilities to see whether --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibilities. We're looking at very minute amounts of glue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And it -- to be fair, it's almost certainly an industry standard type of glue that was used at whatever time that that particular book was used. They're not exactly top-of-the-range books. So it would be a standard type of glue readily available to the industry. Not necessarily to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but this is all speculation on the type --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of glue that's used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The type of glue. Yes, indeed. But I'm sure the experimentation could be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 55 pages are missing throughout the book. Are you able to say anything about the way in which they - above and beyond what you've already said - the way in which they came out of the book?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I really can't tell how they came out of the book. I have little information as to what has happened to these books before they were recovered and seized, after they were recovered and seized, before they came to this court, after they came to this court. There's very little information about them at all, so I have no idea. It -- I think it's less likely that the damage caused to this book is just normal wear and tear and handling and so on, and I think I'm -- and where that is to a certain extent speculation, it is, however, covered by my examination in page forty -- paragraph 45 of book 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we can go to that on the screen, please. 45. Paragraph 45.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This book, Your Honour, is exactly the same format as the book which is book 16. And I've described it again. It has a pocket front and back, and so on and so forth. A separate book. Has a card cover. And the front end paper and the spine have become detached from the block. Now, there's no evidence that any pages are missing and there are no anomalies. And apart from a partial separation of the cover, I can find no other significant anomalies. This book is by and large intact. There are slight damage to the spine, as I have mentioned, but nothing like what we're looking at in page 16, and yet this book is meant to have gone through the same rigors. It's covering a period a little bit before book 16 but it's -- and therefore it's a little bit older than book 16 in terms of chronology of entries, and yet the damage is minimal. And easily explained and, to me, not a problem and no anomalies. So what's -- what's surprising me about book 16 is its complete disintegration, if you like. And I can find no reason for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, then, one question in relation comparing book 12 to book 16. Apparently book 12 is covering a period of less than a month, whereas the other book has been -- is covering a period of two and a half month. So if you say it went through the same - what did you exactly say? - the same rigors, then, at least in time, that is not accurate, as far as the production time is concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. But I'm assuming. And, again, I don't know how this book was -- yes, I do. Book 16 was found inside its leather cover, I believe. It was recovered inside its leather cover. And by that I mean the carpral [phoen] cover had been inserted into the slot at the back. So it was recovered in the way it was meant to be used and the way it has been designed. And the cover, of course, of a book is designed to protect the book. So while it's had another five weeks' writing in it, it -- it -- it's still been used as it was designed. The -- I mean, I'm assuming these original books - and this is an assumption - were designed to be diaries. Therefore, they're meant to last 12 months. In this case, obviously, they lasted two and a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a bit of chicken egg question. The book is damaged so much because it lost its protective covers and that explains why. Or it's the other way around. Where you say it's -- I can't explain how it was so heavily damaged, although you do not know whether it was protected all of the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well as I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, isn't there -- not to say that there may be all kind of explanations, but that there is quite a bit of speculation in whether the damage is the result of a treatment which was different or whether you say, I -- there must be something else, because under similar circumstances you wouldn't accept such large damage. And you said it went through the same rigors. I don't know whether you have any specific knowledge about the rigors 12 and 16 went through when comparing their fate, as far as damage is concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the reason I say it was -- at the time of discovery it was still inside its leather cover. And I don't me just placed inside its leather cover, it was in the right place of its leather cover, and we know that from the scanned photographs. We know the front cover of the -- the carpral cover has been scanned inside and out, and then all the pages, but the back cover wasn't. And yet the leather part of the back cover was. And the only explanation of that is it was not visible because it was inside its leather cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the rigors you are talking about are rigors it went through after they were found.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we know they were all scanned, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But -- but before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What happened --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's the whole point. We don't know what happened before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And it is that period, of course, that I'm interested in. Whatever happened after discovery happened to all of the books in any event, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the -- the same rigors would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- be about that period, then, not about a period before they were discovered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. And it is of course the damage that's caused to the book before they were discovered. That is, obviously, of greater interest, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But we don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I notice the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I apologise. I should have kept an eye on that. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, during my cross-examination I intend to use a chart which summarises the primary findings of the report. I think we could save some time if Mr. Browne were allowed to review that over the course of the break rather than here. It's simply short quotes from the report tied to the different books.
