utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Groome, please provide it to the witness. We take a break, and we resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: A few more questions, Mr. Browne, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go back to your report, 1D05300.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we were dealing with paragraph 55.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You note there that 54 pages are in misalignment with their neighbours. I just want to make sure we understand that precisely. How were those pages within the overall book? Were they affixed to the book or slotted in, or how was it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Well, I think they had once been affixed to a book and glued in, but they were -- they were -- a lot of them were loose. Twenty eight were loose. Fifty four were -- how can I describe it? Let me just see if I can find it in the bundle of photographs that we have, this bundle that's already been provided. The pages have all been printed out by a printer. The measurements and the lines and the spacing and the margins and so on would have been design by the printer, and then all the pages are blocked. They are bound into the spine. And then there're all trimmed. That is the normal way these books are made. I don't think these books were made to order. Particularly, I think they're off of the shelf. Therefore, there's nothing to indicate they've been done specially. And as such, by and large the printed pages will align one to the next to the next, unless for some reason or another they have moved within the book or they have been taken from one book and put into another. That is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How do you distinguish the 28 loose pages from the 54? What's the difference in observation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Well, they're completely separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the 54 are completely separated?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: No, no, no, sorry, the 28 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But then the 54 are attached --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: -- but misaligned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you just develop -- I'm not sure I -- maybe I -- it's only me, but could you just describe that a little more? The 54 are attached but misaligned in the wrong place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: No, sorry. Misaligned as in up and down with their neighbour. The printed line should go straight across like that, and they don't, even though they're stuck into the book, for all intents and purposes what remains of the book. They misalign.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to tell whether that's a result of poor manufacture or later alteration?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I'm not able to tell that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we please identify the specific pages that we are speaking about so I can follow along with the handout?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My problem is which pages have we got here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't know if this could be adjourned to the next break, where Mr. Browne could identify the pages from his -- which -- from his notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Browne thinks that he's better able to answer the question after the next break, we, of course, would accept that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might be advisable using this -- I beg your pardon, I keep forgetting they're there. It might be advisable to do that if nobody minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If that's acceptable to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At 57 you appear to take the matter a bit further. Could you elaborate, or would that depend upon you finding the pages?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: No, it -- basically it's a general comment about the whole of the book. The problem is there are so many loose pages, there are so many pages that are barely attached. I can't establish when those pages were attached or how or in which procedure. The problem with single pages is there's nothing to anchor them to the book. If you've got a set of pages that have an opposite number, a partner, as it were, elsewhere in the book, you've got something to anchor the page so that 1-2 two can be the same piece of paper as 5-6, or something of that nature. Depending on the size of the book, of course, we're dealing with. But if you've just got single sheets, then you take a sheet out, you can put another sheet in. We can't establish what has happened with this book. This is one example, absolutely, where ESDA would have been of huge assistance, because we would be able to see whether the writing on each page had indented into its next page or whether the indentations actually didn't go into that page but went somewhere else and we don't know where they are. And we could have done that with all the -- certainly all the loose pages to see if that was going to render any significant information. It is entirely possible, of course, that it might not have rendered any significant information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you about that same paragraph. You say it would seem that pages have been introduced from elsewhere. Now, is there a possibility that they have got loose from the book, from the original book, and that they are not from elsewhere from -- but from that same book, and after having been loosened, then to be put back again in a similar way as if it would have come from another book or from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, this is where learned counsel for the Prosecution's question is a valid one. Where or how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've not heard of any question -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have read, you have done your homework. That's good, but ... yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- which I will answer properly after the next break, because it's going to need, in the context of the pictures we have, identifying the pages that -- where there is a mismatch. Now, the mismatch couldn't be or shouldn't be wrong, shouldn't be imperfect manufacture. Because once the books are bound together, they're trimmed top and bottom. If the pages are sticking out of the top or bottom, then -- then that isn't the way they were manufactured. If they've been put back in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- they may have been put back in during usage, but if they are in the right place and the lines mis-- you know, the printing misaligns significantly, then that is an indication they could have come from another book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But they could come from the same book as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could, that it has been badly put together, it has been badly manufactured. I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We just start now. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash. Oh. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise. I haven't read this yet. So when I put some of the questions that you intend to put, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I think what the witness was referring to when I suggested that it would be helpful to know which pages he's referring to, I think that's what the witness was referring to. And can I just say before -- while we're talking about this, that can the witness be advised that we have all the pages of that book in e-court, although we only have a certain selection here. So he should not feel bound just to this, but simply he can check his notes and let us know which pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We'll be providing him with a full copy of the Cyrillic over the break, with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move on from this book to one other book. Book 21. You deal with this at paragraph 70 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have that on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to try to understand --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. Can we have a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We're there on the screen, actually. Paragraph 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Book 21, you note that it relates to the 2008 seizure. And a single page has been removed, page 543. This appears to be in the middle of a meeting.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we go to paragraph 71, you note that the book appears to have been completely -- completed almost entirely within the chronological lifetime of book 20 above.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And perhaps if you are able to demonstrate your observations on this by reference to the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen, please, P394. English page 11, B/C/S page 16. And B/C/S 0649-0536. And for Your Honours' information: Book 21, parts of book 21, have been exhibited under P394, pages forty -- exhibited by the Prosecution, of P394, page 42, 72 to 73, 124 to 125, 140 to 141, 189 to 190, 204 to 210, and 263 to six -- 268. And I just want to assist, if I can, Your Honours a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So this reference in your report to page 543 missing and appearing to be in the middle of a meeting. This is a meeting, it seems, in Belgrade on the 30th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we go over the page to page 13 of the English and 16 of the B/C/S -- sorry, let's go to page 12, because we can see that - page 12 of the English and 17 of the B/C/S - where apparently, allegedly, Stanisic is there and claims, as we can see -- its alleged that he is talking about men from Banja Luka. And then over the page to page 13 of the English and 18 of the B/C/S, he's alleged to have said: "We have been supplying 100.000 men for six months. There is poor organisation in RS. They plundered us." And then if we go to page 15 of the English and 20 of the B/C/S, Stanisic is alleged to have said: "I can find 120 perfect men who would come there in seven days." And then he's alleged to have said: "They should not be engaged (we gave 80 from Erdut, we gave 80 from Deletovci ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, before we return to the report, if we can look on the left side of the screen at the Cyrillic, and I think it's accepted that CM refers to Milosevic and JC refers to Stanisic. And we have a change, it appears there, from CM apparently saying: "They should not be engaged (we gave 80 from Erdut, we gave 80 to Deletovci ..." and then that's changed to JC. So are you able to say anything about that, Mr. Browne? If you can't, you can't. The change from Milosevic to Stanisic, there.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Nothing showed up on the infrared and -- the infrared lighting which would indicate that a different ink had been used to make that alteration. And therefore, it's -- there's nothing I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: It may be the same pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's go back to your conclusion about a missing page, page 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we could go to page 54-- the actual page 543 in the Cyrillic, which should be English page 18, B/C/S 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just so you can explain what, in fact, you were saying when you said that page 543 was missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which paragraph in the report are we at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 70, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What am I looking at on the screen here, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not sure, actually, either. You should be looking at --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is B/C/S ERN 0649 to 0543.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I have got 595 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yup, so have I.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Should I repeat the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's wait for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We would prefer e-court page, because it's difficult to navigate through actual pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's English page 18 and B/C/S page 23. Sorry, I know what the problem is. Could we go back, please, to English page 17 and B/C/S page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you, while this is coming up, explain exactly what you mean by this -- why -- how you observed a single page had been removed? And ...

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. These books are manufactured as a series of books stuck together, Your Honour. We have a series of books of a few pages in each case, and then they are stuck together. But each separate book is sewn together. And if you tear a page out, of course, these pages all have, as it were, a brother on the other side of the spine. And if you take one page away, you leave one page behind, and that is what I'm looking at here. That page 542 is on a completed pair, then we get to the stitches, and then page 543 is all that's left, as it were. The original page 543 has been torn out. Now, there's -- and thus it is missing. It has to be said, of course, that page -- the missing page does not appear to have impacted or had anything to do with the meeting of the 30th of June, as far as I can make out. It had finished before the beginning -- the end of page 542.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to avoid confusion, and perhaps there's a mistake, but Mr. Jordash does realise that page 543 is not part of P394. I don't know if he appreciates that. But as far as I know, this particular page we're talking about is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that I had just realised that and was going to deal with it via that explanation and then move on. But thank you to Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that will do for that explanation, Mr. Browne, for my purposes. Let's move to your final conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I ask one question. If a page is torn out, that means that then two pages are missing, both sides of that sheet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we are talking about one missing page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One missing half-sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half-sheet, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's a more accurate description --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of what we're talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move back to your report, Mr. Browne. 1D05300. Paragraph 80, you note that the writing throughout the books appears neat and small and orderly.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: That's what it appears. I can't read Cyrillic, but that's -- the writing does seem to be neat and compact and orderly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you shown, as part of the preparation for your report, a handwriting report prepared for the Seselj case by Dorijan Kerzan?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I was. Because it covered the authorship of the handwriting, and effectively just disposed of it from my point of view, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we intend to tender this, Your Honour, but with agreement with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And he notes at page 12 that the handwriting of the disputed notes is fluent. Legibility is very good. The writer has an excellent writing skill, and the control of the pen is excellent as well. Mistakes in writing are very rare. Did you agree with that assessment, Mr. Browne?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I think it sums up probably in better language than I did it. But yes, throughout the books that I've looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And paragraph 80, you go on to say you consider there must be rough notes made at the time. What are you trying to say there, precisely?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Well, these book are meant to be, as far as I'm instructed, they're meant to be diaries. They were written throughout -- across a period of a number of years by, as I understand it, a senior military officer. They are, if you like, his working diaries. They contain minutes of meetings, as a part of my instructions, and notes of other matters. I don't know what those minutes are, what they say, what the words say. But they go -- we have a large number of books written by hand throughout. I would expect -- so neatly, I would expect that there would be rough notes from which these notes, these diaries, could then be compiled. And there's nothing wrong with that. That's a perfectly reasonable thing. But a sight of the rough notes would have been very useful because that would show how the person actually writes at speed, and then he returns to whatever room he uses to write his diary and transcribes. I can say this because I've used -- I've examined a lot of police notebooks in my time, and have been notes of interviews and so on, and I have been able to give evidence that the books were used -- the books, those notes, were written up having used rough notes first. And that -- that's what these diaries seem to appear like for me. There are no rough notes. They are very, very neat throughout. And there is nothing in them that indicates they'd been written in action, if you like. And I don't mean under shell fire, as in the working context of a senior military officer. The writing is all his, so the report tells us, and I have no reason to doubt that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've got no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Browne.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Could I ask one additional question in relation to the last matter. You say: "And there is nothing in them that indicates they had been written in action." Is there anything which indicates that they were not written in action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their neatness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's exactly that. It's their neatness, their -- it's considered handwriting. It is neat. Somebody has thought about it and they have put it in -- on paper. And as I say, there's nothing inherently wrong with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But it wasn't -- it's not during the rough and tumble of a meeting, with people giving their opinions, and so on and so forth, and coming out. It's all very neatly laid out again and again and again. That is where -- where that's -- where I'm coming from with that. And Mr. Kerzan points it out as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you refer to your experience, because I'm trying to find out what exactly the basis for this conclusion is. You said: "I have seen notes of interviews and I have been able to give --" and there the transcript is not very clear. But at least it indicates that you were able to establish that there had been rough notes first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I had expressed as part of my conclusions in the original part of the cases where I was involved in this sort of work, an officer has said, No, I made these notes verbatim at the time. And so on. And I have examined them and said, No, this is too even, this is too smooth, this is too neat, if you like. And there must have been rough notes. And then eventually the officer is re-interviewed and he admits he had rough notes and he produced them. Now, in some of those cases it didn't matter a bit that he had rough notes. He just was foolish to not admit that there they were and here they were. But, yeah, it's people who are writing in notebooks and writing minutes, as it were, are writing under a certain amount of pressure. And there's nothing in these -- in the way this writing, even though it is Cyrillic, there's nothing in the way of this writing that indicates that the person has been writing terribly quickly, that the person has been writing under any sort of, not duress, but the pressure of making sure he's got everything down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this still within your field of expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is more or less psychology, isn't it? That where the people are able to remain fully calm and control their writing speed. I'm just wondering whether there's any scientific basis for this conclusion. Is there any publication about neatness is always a indication that it has been copied? Is there any -- any source which would support your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's source -- there's The Forensic Science Society, the ASQDE. I can't quote the actual source of these, but there have been studies carried out as to the deterioration of writing under speed. In the immigration service we did it ourselves. We had to carry out a study for internal use only as to write -- officers having to write in notebooks. And that was in the days before we began to tape-record all our interviews, because we had to try and maintain the flow of the interview and yet record what was being said in that interview as accurately as we could, and how the writing deteriorated the faster people we were interviewing spoke. And it's nothing really to do with the psychology. It's nothing really to do with the -- a -- with duress or anything like that. It's just the business of trying to get the information down on a piece of paper accurately as you can, and then you write it up afterwards neatly yourself. And we found that what we were trying to do in my office was to try and find out an armament for getting tape recorders in rather than carrying on writing in notebooks. And that is one of the things. If duress doesn't really come into it and stress doesn't come into it, because we know those things don't actually affect the way somebody writes or signs their name, but the actual need for speed is the determinator, as were, of slight deterioration. There's also more chance you might have misheard, you make a mistake, you go back, you alter it. And making the books neat from rough notes is much more -- in my view, it's an acceptable explanation as to the neatness of these books throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although we -- do we have any information about the urgency and the speed needed if written in action or if copied? I can imagine that someone who has a busy job to do, being in a high military position, that copying would put him under similar time pressure as the jotting down what he observed during the meeting. I mean, do we know anything about that, or is it just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything about it at all. That's the point. I mean, I can only make the observation having examined the books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But would you agree with me that it, your conclusion, is based on an assumption? Neatness should mean here, this and this and this. Whereas, not knowing the circumstances under which they were either drafted at a later stage on the basis of rough notes or that are written down immediately is circumstances are totally unknown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's -- this is -- this is the problem, one of the problems. We do not know enough about these books in any event, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but your conclusions is rather firm. It must be, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would -- I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me check, because I -- I'm now quoting from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paragraph 80.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- my memory. "I consider there must be rough notes." Which is a pretty strong conclusion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But I can tell you that that number of books written over that period so neatly all the way through, as commented on by Dr. Kerzan as well, is an indication that they were written in a considered way. Otherwise, the meetings would take a very long time, I think. But it's -- that is a throw-away remark. I can't tell how fast he wrote any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I hear you say implicitly that on the basis of your observations that you consider it likely or very likely that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I consider it likely there would be rough notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's different from: There must be rough notes. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll agree to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.text: May I tender some documents before I sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps an example of why I'm having such difficulty. So there's a picture that we saw of books piled on top of each other. utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 80 -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's just that I'm -- I mean -- I don't know, maybe the Chamber -- maybe I'm the only one having this difficulty. utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D3482 will receive number D776, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And 1D05471 is a statement -- another statement by -- from Ms. Gallagher taken by the Stanisic Defence team with the Prosecution present during the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5471 will receive number D777, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jordash, have we looked at that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, we haven't, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It sounds that it could be a document which is produced for the purposes of the proceedings before this Tribunal, which, of course, usually triggers the applicability of Rule 92 bis, 92 ter, et cetera. utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it raises this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I beg your pardon, Your Honour, I should have showed it to you. It's a note of an interview with Ms. Gallagher which has been agreed by Ms. Gallagher and agreed by the Prosecution as representing an accurate record of a interview relating solely to her knowledge of the chain of custody of these notebooks, from Serbian government custody to ICTY Prosecution custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I raised a purely procedural issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And given the substance, I would not take the procedural point, although I do recognise that the Chamber is correct. It would be ordinary subject to Rule 92 bis or ter. But the Prosecution does not take that procedural point and is happy to have it before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And due to the possibility of serving as precedent, I think the Chamber would need its time, look at it first, before we decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, D777 is marked for identification. Please proceed. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a word of caution with respect to the Serbian documents. I don't know if Mr. Jordash has informed them that he would be tendering these or whether any of those interests are implicated with these documents. I just raise it for the Chamber's consideration as to whether or not we need to be cautious in how those documents are tendered at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From Jordash is tendering it. He has an opportunity, if he has not done so yet, to consider whether any protective measures for those documents should be sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we would like to hear from you within 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, that may be tricky to get an answer so quickly, but they've never indicated to us that they regarded these documents as something which fell into the category that they'd been concerned with before. I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If you try to make up your mind as soon as possible. Even if it would not be within the 24 hours, but preferably to be done not later than tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. And then finally, 1D05472, which is the protocol that was agreed upon for Mr. Browne's examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the protocol would receive number ...
