utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, are you ready to start your cross-examination? It will be only for the next, I would say, next ten minutes approximately, because then we'll take a break. But if you're ready, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Defence has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Browne, I don't have to explain to you who Mr. Petrovic is, but he is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Mr. Groome --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- are you ready to start your cross-examination, although for a limited number of minutes at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Mr. Browne, I have forgotten to introduce Mr. Groome to you, but he is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Browne.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me begin by just asking you to comment on one of the sentences from your conclusion section of your report, now in evidence as D769. You say, and it's the second full paragraph after, "in my opinion": "The chronology of the books is such that no reliance can be placed on their veracity." Is it your conclusion that the Chamber should not place any reliance on the veracity of any of the books that you examined?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Well, the problem is, the books appear to stand off all together, to a certain extent. They've -- they've always been presented, as it were to me, as a set. And there is -- there are problems with continuity, anyway, as far as I'm aware from the documents served. Now, I fully accept that the Defence and the Prosecution -- I beg your pardon, may not have felt the need to furnish me with certain details as to continuity, and that's fair enough. That's none of my business. We do have this issue of the entries, the neatness of the entries throughout. We also have books that appear to have -- be running tandem with other books, and I can't think of an explanation for this. If you've got books -- so this is a diary of events, this is -- these books are one long diary of events, to all intents and purposes, covering a period of time. I cannot understand why there would be a need to start a second book and then revert to the previous book again later on. And as such, then, if you've got books that are written out of order, we don't know which books have been written out of order. And, therefore, if we don't know which books were written out of order, how can we accept any of them without some sort of chain of evidence or custody that we can work off?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that it's beyond the reasonable possibility that any of these books could be accurate and authentic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: As a whole, I think the whole concept of them being a record from beginning to end, in chronological order, as a diary of events from then to then, as a whole, I think the whole concept is flawed. Now, what weight that -- that carries, I am unable to say, because that's really not for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me see if I can clarify a bit further. In your work examining passports, if you came across a passport that maybe had the stamps of ten different countries in there, and in your examination of those stamps you identified one that you were quite certain was a forgery, would that mean that you would consider all of the stamps in that passport forgeries?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I wouldn't need to consider the rest, because once you've got a forged stamp in a passport, the whole passport becomes a forgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So now --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: It's a false instrument.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try to clearly distinguish there. At this moment I think we are to some extent mixing up legal qualifications with facts. If you say one false stamp makes the whole of the passport a forgery, then from a legal point of view that may be true, but that's not, I think, what Mr. Groome was in -- was asking you, whether it would mean that the other stamps would been forgeries in themselves as well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there we should not mix up --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- normal type of questions with factual questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, and I beg Mr. Groome's pardon. The -- of course not. If we're examining a whole series of stamps, and one is demonstrably a forgery, and we can give evidence on that, it doesn't render all the other stamps in the -- in that particular passport forgeries. Of course. No matter what effect it has on the whole document, or the document as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've just said with respect to the analogy that I gave you with respect to the stamps in the passport: "I wouldn't need to consider the rest, because once you've got a forged stamp in a passport, the whole stamp [sic] becomes -- it's a false instrument."

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: No, the whole passport is a false instrument.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is that not the same analysis that you've applied here? That once you found book 16, which caused you serious concern, you essentially now have dismissed all the remaining notebooks as being unreliable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Could I -- I don't think that's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, could you -- I don't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I beg your pardon, sorry. I object to whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I think that -- whether that's what the witness said or not, but he's fully competent to explain whether Mr. Groome did understand his words well or not. That's apparently your concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, and I was just going to refer the Chamber to -- [microphone not activated] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome, could you please repeat, possibly rephrase, your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm wondering how it is that your concerns with respect to 16, book 16, would cause you to give an opinion, let's say, with respect to book 2, which is a book that you've accepted as the handwriting of Mr. Mladic, and you found no anomalies in that book. I'm trying to understand how you reached the conclusion to -- that no reliance should be placed on the veracity of what's in book number two based upon what you found in book number 16.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Um, it -- the -- it's -- it's not as such what I have said. The -- in the paragraph you're referring, which I've now lost again. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to book 2, it's paragraph 21.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Oh, no, yeah, I was going back to the original point. You're saying that book 16 nullifies the whole thing. In the paragraph we're talking about in my conclusion, which is what started your line of inquiry, the chronology of the books is such that the problem is, if I have found -- oh, it's not something I have found. This is the chronology. It's there to be seen from the entries in the books. It's not something that I've been terribly clever about. The chronology, if you have books that overlap, that overlapping affects in a ripple effect all the way down the chain, as it were, because we -- we don't know which was the one that was started or which is the one that has -- which, as it were, is the original book that was abandoned and then rejoined or which is the book that has been written ... we have no way of knowing what the real physical chronology of the book rather than the datal chronology of the books are. So we don't know which are the original books, which have been rewritten, which have been written in tandem. We know there are tandem books. That's a matter from the dates within the books. We know there are tandem books in running, but we don't know which came first. It's a chicken and egg to a certain extent. And that must ripple down the whole chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is your conclusion based upon an assumption that if there are two books being recorded into during the same time-period, that there must be something suspicious about all of the books?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I don't think we can ignore that possibility, because we don't know which order they were written in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: And it's not just, sort of, one book overlaps another. There are some books that overlap three books. And how far back down does this go?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Have you considered the possibility that perhaps one book was used, let's say, in the main office of the Main Staff and perhaps another book may have been used carried by a driver and used in the field? Have you considered that that might be a logical explanation for multiple books during the same time-period?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to me to be terribly logical. Purely and simply because, as I understand it, in my imperfect understanding of Mladic's position in the world, although I understand he's a very senior general, his staff are going to go with him, for a start. They are with him. The books aren't that bad -- big that he needs to have one with his driver and one with the other staff. And the fact is, he writes them all. We -- that's common ground, I think, that he is the author of the books. Why would he spread them around for various members of staff to carry for him? It doesn't make much logical sense to me, to be fair. I'm not denying that it couldn't be the case, but it doesn't make much logical sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this logic within your field of expertise, to say that how a general keeps his diaries at one place or another or give it to his driver, as suggested by Mr. Groome? I'm just wondering what the basis for your, although cautious, conclusion is that it's illogical to do it this way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my father was a professional soldier and a senior officer, but apart from that, very little. The observations -- the observations as to the chronology is just a matter of observation. I don't have to be a document expert to be all to see that the dates overlap. And indeed that information has been there for -- ever since the books were discovered, and any side - Prosecution or Defence - could have seen these. It's obviously they came out in some stark relief and it's only when you put the books into chronological order that you realise there are problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, looking at your evidence, you said: "So we don't know which are the original books."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which suggests that there's one original and another one which is not original; whereas in the assumption of Mr. Groome, there are two originals. You say: Which have been rewritten. Which is a pure assumption that one of them has been rewritten and the other not or -- I mean, that's all -- sounds rather speculative. And nevertheless, that's the kind of questions you raise on what you say is a simple observation on the chronology as we find it in the diaries itself. But you draw by far more questions from that, with all kind of implicit assumptions. That there is one who is rewritten and that there is one original and the other one should not be original. But it's still to be established. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would to a certain extent, Your Honour. Yes, of course, you're correct. But I would consider that one thing's for sure: They can't have been written together, as it were, at the same time. He's only got one hand with the pen. But we -- I -- and of course this comment is made without knowledge of what the writing says, and I don't know if any of the books have been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All of the books have been translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of the books have been translated. Then obviously page by page it is simply to see what the books refer to in each case. Something that is not for me. Other people can do that, of course, and will undoubtedly have done so. But the fact is, we don't know which book was started before another. We don't know. And your comment is absolutely right, of course, Your Honour. We don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome. No, I'm looking at the clock --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we should take a break. Unless you have one --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask just one or two questions, just -- the issue is very ripe now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking at the Stanisic Defence. One or two questions for Mr. Groome, or should we put them after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We could continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Browne, while we're on the topic and while it's foremost on our minds, did you ever ask the Stanisic Defence whether translations of the diary entries revealed that they were two different versions of the same event or two different versions of the same meeting recorded in the overlapping books? Did you ever ask for that information?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would that have been important information to have at your disposal before drawing the conclusion that the fact that they were concurrent books was per se evidence of an authenticity problem with the books?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Almost certainly it might have had a bearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can leave it there for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take a break, and we resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, if you're ready you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Browne, your last answer before the break with respect to having information about duplicate recordings of the same event, you said: "Almost certainly it might have had a bearing." Can I ask you to accept my representation that there are no duplicate entries for the same meeting or same event, and can I now ask you what bearing does it have on your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: That -- that a number of books have been used out of sequence. I don't know what the -- the ultimate significance is, but I will accept that if there is absolutely no duplication, then I have no other explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would you maintain your conclusion that I first began to address with you, that the chronology -- chronology of the books is such that no reliance can be placed on their veracity? Would you maintain that conclusion or would this information have a bearing on that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: It is bound to have a bearing on the -- I'm sorry, I'm lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is on page 12 of your report. It's in the conclusion section. And it's the second full paragraph of that section.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yeah, sorry. I was looking at the screen. It's not there. That's all right. Yeah. I beg your pardon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So perhaps you could reword that or paraphrase your conclusion so we can understand what bearing it would have.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I still say there must be some doubts cast upon the chronology of these books. But I still can't -- I'm trying to -- sorry, I'm trying to reword what you asked me to do. But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Maybe just redraft --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm trying to do. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- only that first sentence.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: -- beg your pardon. I beg your pardon. If I was going to redraft it, then I would say the chronology of the books is such that a limited reliance can be placed on their veracity rather than no reliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could ask for your assistance in understanding another conclusion that you draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if we could go to e-court page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I could draw your attention to paragraph 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The last sentence of paragraph 82 states: "It also raises the question as to which books were written contemporaneously and which were written after the event - neatly." Do I take from this sentence that you consider that some of the books were written contemporaneously and that some of the books were written after the fact? Is that what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Well, this paragraph is based on the fact that we have -- we have information that the -- form the print -- printing of the books that they were manufactured years before and therefore they'd been held, presumably empty, before they were actually brought into use. And we know of the ability to start books in parallel, therefore there are a great many more books than we seem to need if we were going to deal with this. And in it raises the question -- obviously it raises the question as to contemporaneity, and this has to be taken into account with the handwriting which is neat throughout. And there is a question relating to the contemporaneous nature of the entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, we can see that in your report, and what I'm trying to understand with some degree of precision: Is it your evidence that all of the books that you examined were written after the fact, or is it your evidence, as is suggested by this sentence, that some of the books were written contemporaneously and some were written after the event?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I think it is my evidence that we can't -- I certainly cannot exclude the possibility that the books were not written contemporaneously and that they were written out neatly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that all of the books, in your view, were written after the fact?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes. And we don't know -- and it's not possible, therefore, to date any of the actual writings, no matter what the date of the event that is being recorded or reported on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you undertook during the break to identify to us the pages in book number 16 that are misaligned and that are missing or that are detached from the book?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I have to report that I haven't finished my homework, Your Honour. And I apologise for that. But the entries -- there are too many entries for me to have done it in the time. I can tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we do the following, then --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, could I ask you to identify those pages as best you can now --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- and then perhaps with the Court's permission you be allowed to keep whatever you need overnight and finish your homework, as it were?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yeah. Certainly. I've gone up to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we do that, can I ask one question.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Certainly. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I had expected that you would have had this in your notes, this information. Is it not a matter of simply referring --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's in my notes. But I'm demonstrating pictorially what I was talking about, from these scans is what I've just been -- making sure they matched up. They are in my notes. I have loads of notes on this book, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So then can we proceed in the following way: Could I ask you to right now look at your notes and tell us which pages were misaligned and then which ones were missing, and then tomorrow we'll ask you -- I'll ask you or give you an opportunity to actually show us the pages and how you came to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the misaligned pages first, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Right. Let me just make sure I'm talking the -- yes, we are. These -- this book -- the scans start -- effectively, the first page is 4212.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we use the number that the prefix is J. And I think that's the --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: That is. That is. 4212.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: But it's -- they all start with J000.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, so at least that we're clear on that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please do not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's my fault. I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We shouldn't overlap, otherwise there's difficulty in translating.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I apologise. So the first one which is misaligned is 2134, which is 4213 and 4214.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If we could stop there for a second. So can you please explain exactly what that means?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: What, to misalign with the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. So you're saying that 2134 is in between pages 2-- 4213 and 4214; is that --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: No, I beg your pardon. The misalignment occurs between 4213 and 4214.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And 2134, is that of any --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: No, no, there is no number -- sorry. All the numbers begin with a 4. 4213 and 4214.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: The two pages belong together and they don't align.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: 4215 and 4216. 4223 and 4224. 4225, 4226. 4227 and 4228. 4229 and 4230. 4231, 4232. 4233 and 4234. 4235, 4236. 4237 and 4238. 4239 and 4240. 4241, 422-- sorry, 4242. 4243, 4244. Then we come into an area where there is some loose pages in the middle of it, which don't help.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can stop you there. Are these the pages that are barely attached or are these the pages that are completely disassociated from the book?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: The loose pages are disassociated with the book, but they've been scanned in the order they appear, so they have to be taken that way, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you do that, then just tell us that they are completely detached.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Indeed. Okay, so we have 4248 is detached, and you can't see it from the -- from the scans, but it matches with 4247, which is attached. 4249, which is, of course, the other side of 4248, doesn't match with 4250.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you how you came to the conclusion that 42 -- that 4248 matched 4247?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: It's an manual thing. We've got a loose page. It's manual. I place it so that the top matches the bottom and then compare the printing lines across, as it were. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It does. But that -- is it possible -- do you know if the text from one page carries over onto the next page?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I have no -- I have not noted any handwriting that goes across a spine, a seem, from one page to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: If that makes sense. I beg your pardon. Where was I - 4250?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Not a good match with 4249, which was the loose page. There's a loose page, 4251, and that's okay with 4252. 4253 doesn't align with 4254. 4257 doesn't align with 4258. 4261 doesn't align with 4262. 4263 doesn't align with 4264.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And again, just so that we're clear: These pages are now attached back in the book, they just -- they were --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: They were -- they were attached at the time I did the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What's the first -- the first one that's now attached but misaligned -- if you could -- in this series?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon. 5354.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I will tell you when there's a loose page, because you asked me to. So -- and if I don't mention whether it's loose, it isn't. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Understood. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Now I'm lost again, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: 4263 was the last number you were on.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Thank you. It doesn't align with 4264. 4265 doesn't align with the loose 4266. But the other side of 4266, which is 4267, does align with 4268, which is affixed -- it is attached, sorry. Is that what I said: 4267 with 4268, that alines, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's what you -- yes, that's how you're recorded.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- sorry. 4269 does not align with 4270. 4271 and 4272 do not align. 4273 and 4274 do not align. 4275 and 4276 do not align. 4277 and 4278 do not align. But - and this is a case where a page has partially become detached but is not fully attached - 4277 matched 4280; in other words, the page -- a couple of pages down and the one in the middle is the one that doesn't work. But you can't see it from the scans. It's -- it's there when you lift that part of the page. We have a loose 4282, which doesn't match with 4281. And the loose 4283, which is the other side, doesn't match with 4284 - 84 is affixed. 4285 does not match 4286. And 4285 is good with, actually, 4288, but you can't see that from the -- the scan. And 4287 doesn't match with 4288. 4293 does not match 4294. But there's a loose 4296 which does match 4293, but you can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask, just in the interest of time: How many more pages do you -- do you think you will be telling us?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm looking for a pen behind my ear, but I can't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just an approximate number.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: About twenty -- between 25 and 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the Court approves, perhaps it would been an expeditious use of time just to ask the witness overnight to write down these numbers rather than spend the next 45 minutes going through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the other parties. There seems to be no objection. Not only homework during the day, Mr. Browne, but homework at night as well. Would you follow this suggestion? Are you willing to follow this suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question in between. If you look at the other books, like book 12 or whatever, do you see bad alignment within those books where note pages seem to have been loose from the book? I mean, to what extent is it specific for partly or even entirely loosened pages to have bad alignment? Or does this happen in the -- in the unaffected or the still integral books. And I think this is a question which is related to some extent to what Mr. Jordash asked you, that is, whether we can form any opinion as to bad production or any tampering at a later stage. Could you tell us whether you found any bad alignments in books which were otherwise without suspicion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In some of the cases where the books have been bound by thread, Your Honour, and some of the earlier books in the sequence that I examined, it was possible to show that batches of the pages, where they connected, because they obviously come from a different production line, or a different part of the production line, that's what I would put it down to. In my experience, sometimes they marginally miss, but there was no evidence of the book being dismantled. There was no evidence of tampering at all. And it was reasonable to say that that is a production fault in those -- in those cases, and therefore it's not an anomaly and it was of no concern to me at all. The difference in this book and the difference -- and -- and book 12, I think it is, in my evidence, is that we -- this book is one of the only two books that have single pages anyway. And it's also one of the few books that's actually exploded, almost, to -- to -- for whatever reason, is in bits. And therefore there is a greater significance. Because it's single pages, it is so easy to take them out and put them in from another book of a similar manufacture, but the bulk of the books have been sewn together and therefore didn't cause me any concern at all. I didn't consider any slight differences there as being significant, because there was no evidence of other tampering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does that mean that you did not find in the comparable book 12 any misalignment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't answer that. I do apologise. No. I didn't note any misalignment within that. There was just the beginning of the -- the first page that had been -- was still on the cover had split from the rest of the book and -- and that was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you specifically looked for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did go back and look at that when it came to the comparison, and there were no anomalies noted in book 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me be sure that I understand your evidence correctly. When you say "misaligned" --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Many of the pages, the evidence numbers, are consecutive. So my question to you is: The pages that are -- the lines that are misaligned, are they the front and back of the same piece of paper or are they on adjacent pages?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: It's the alignment between adjacent pages. Not front/back. That -- I mean, front and back have been printed in the same go, as it were, and it's the alignment between that page and that page. Not that page and that page. If that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, did you compare the alignment, not between the adjacent page, but every second page? So, for example, did you check the alignment between pages ending 65, 67, 69, 71, as it were, all the odd pages? Did you check the alignment between the odd pages or the odd-printed surfaces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: You mean one with the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: If they were attached, that's very difficult to do, because you would have to detach them to make that comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You wouldn't be able to bend the pieces of paper over to look and see whether they line up?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Not with incurring the displeasure of the NFI person, because the risk of the book being further damaged. But yes, where a book had become partly -- a page had become partly detached, it was possible to just carefully move it aside so that we could see whether there was a cross-match between that page. And I mentioned a couple, when I was reading out, that that page still matched that one but didn't match the one in between, if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me see if I can clarify: So is it your evidence that the odd pages align with the odd pages, and the even-numbered pages align with the even-numbered pages, they just didn't align with each other?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: No, no. That's -- that is too simplistic, frankly. Sometimes it was possible to see through the -- as it were, through the spine, behind the spine, to show that odd and even matched each other between certain pages but didn't match the pages -- the single page that was in between. So, Your Honour, it would be wrong -- I mean, there were plenty of odd pages that matched the even pages. They're the numbers I haven't read out. It's just I have only reported on the anomalies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you this question: Can you appreciate that for those involved in this trial and are considering what weight can be placed upon the substance written on pages in this book, that it would be very important for us to know whether that page is actually attached to a book or appears to be a loose page inserted into the book?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I then ask you why you don't in your report identify the numbers now that we're going through? Why is that not in your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I can only apologise for that. Partly a time issue. And that's -- that's effectively it, really. I should have put them in. I can appreciate that is the case. I should have done that, but I didn't, and I apologise to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to leave this topic for now and just want to gain a basic understanding of your background and your experience. As I understand from your report, as it pertains to your background, you worked for the immigration service of the United Kingdom for 21 years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, 22, in fact, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you describe that position in annex A of your report as having involved "the forensic examination, including handwriting, of a variety of documents for evidence of fraud, including passports, identity cards, driving licences, certificates, and company papers." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Then am I correct that some people seeking to enter the United Kingdom unlawfully or remain there unlawfully would alter documents fraudulently to deceive the immigration service?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: They would probably be in possession -- could well be in possession of fraudulent documents, yes. Whether they physically altered them, I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in possessing such falsified documents, their intention was to misrepresent their identity or something about themselves, such as place of birth or employment; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that for as long as governments have issued and relied on identity documents, people have tried to falsify them?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: The earliest I know of is 1236. But, yeah, I accept that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So from 1236 you know, as an expert, that people have been trying to falsify identity documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Whether it's a 15-year-old who wants to have a beer in a pub or a terrorist seeking entry unlawfully into a country under an assumed name to commit a serious crime.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that governments and private organisations that issue identification documents are continually looking for ways to make their documents harder to falsify?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes. Because there's one absolute standard, and that is: There is no such thing as an unforgeable document. So they always have to try and keep going with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And over the years security features are introduced in an effort to stay ahead of what a clever forger might be able to do with a colour printer and a laminating machine?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Features such a holograms, micro printing, unique custom-made papers, printing that is only visible under special lighting - these would be some of the techniques that would be used; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your work for the UK immigration service has been to use your skill, experience, and knowledge of these security features to identify falsified identification documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Identification documents, yes. And any other document that happens to be carried or being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your specialised training, skill, and experience is more than what the ordinary immigration officer staffing the immigration desk at Stansted Arrivals would have, although that person would have some basic training in identifying suspicious documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you evaluate an identification document which you know should have a security feature, would it be fair to say that you look for the presence or absence of that security feature?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if you know that the passport or a passport should have a picture of the Queen or some text printed in ink that is only visible under black light, you place the document under black light to see whether you can see that image; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if you cannot see it, you know that it's a falsified document.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: It would be one of the things one would look at and one of the things one would take into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, am I also correct in saying that any difference is per se evidence of fraud. There is no legitimate reason for a person to change the date of birth on their passport, is there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Not that I have come across, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So finding an anomaly in a document with security features is per se evidence that the person is attempting to perpetrate a fraud?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Well, when I used the train immigration officers to look at documents, we always said you had to collect the anomalies and see if they were mutually inexplicable, because sometimes an anomaly might -- there might be a possibility of an explanation. You gather all the anomalies, you put them together, you see what you've got, and you write your report as to the fact that the document is false.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I were to hand you an ordinary piece of paper, purporting to be a letter from Mr. Jones, generated on a standard computer printer, it would have no security features or litmus test that you could rely on; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's a fundamentally different job, isn't it, to determine whether that letter written on an ordinary piece of computer paper is a -- is a falsified document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Absolutely. We would have to have reference material.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that your -- your job as someone trying to detect whether it's falsified is appreciably more difficult in that scenario?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes. It depends what the question is, doesn't it, really? It's [indiscernible] just holding up one piece of paper and saying, Here's a letter, prove it's false. We would -- the first thing we would say is, No. But we would ask for information, we would ask for background, we would ask for reference documents with which to compare.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And aren't the type of documents I'm now referring to fundamentally different from documents with built in security features in that an anomaly in these documents could be the product of a deliberate effort to commit a fraud or could have some innocent and non-fraudulent reason for the anomaly?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: We'd have to find the anomaly. In the case of -- I'm sorry, I've forgotten the name, Mr. Jones was it? His letter. We would have to be pointed to what the suspicion was and then we would know what we could do or couldn't do to complete the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So let's say that the letter from Mr. Jones said my birth-date is the 21st of March, 1970, and then it was crossed out and a different date was put there, that wouldn't be per se evidence of fraud. It could also be evidence that Mr. Jones or whoever prepared the letter made a mistake, an honest mistake, in recording his date of birth?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed. That's why we'd need the background information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that's a fundamental difference from Mr. Jones's passport where if the date of his birth is altered on that document, we know that there's been a --

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if we look at your examination of the Jankovic diaries, you noted 17 examples where dates had been altered, and you did this at paragraph 14 of your report.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And although these alterations are numerous, you don't consider them per se indications of fraud, and consider that there may be an innocent explanation; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: That is because it's the only book that I examined, isn't it? Isn't that what I say? What paragraph? I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Paragraph 14 of your report is where you deal with this particular part of the Jankovic ...

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yeah. It's -- I can't comment. As you see in paragraph 50, I'm unable to interpret the Cyrillic writing and thus can't comment on the significance of the alternated dates. I can't. They've been altered by perhaps one day. They've been altered in the same pen, with the same ink. What can I say? I have no other books with which to compare. All I've done is noted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You don't have anything in the conclusion of your report with respect to the Jankovic diaries in that conclusion section on page 12. Is there any significance to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: None at all. I must admit I didn't -- I didn't. I didn't conclude anything from it, frankly. I had nothing with which to compare. I have noted what I found. And it wasn't possible to go any further. All right, I accept I should have put that in as a separate conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, just so the record is clear: What the your conclusion with respect to the Jankovic diary?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I'm unable to interpreter the significance of my findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Earlier today you said the following, and I've -- I apologise that I don't have the transcript reference handy. You said: There's no difference if it's a security document as a passport or whether it's an ordinary handwritten notebook or diary. And you were referring to examinations of the book. Do you want to revise that in light of your testimony over the last few minutes about the differences between security documents and other documents without security features?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Well, if we're going -- if I can go back to the Jones letter. I have said that you need reference material. You need -- if I was going to examine Jones -- it depends what the question is, frankly. What are you trying to say? Is the signature forged, or is the letter per se a forgery? Has it been written with the wrong date? Or whatever. If it's a matter of, We don't trust this letter -- and this does happen a lot in litigation, where one party will turn around and say, Well that's all very convenient, having a letter that says X, Y, and Z, but we don't believe either that the letter was written then. We think it was written just for the purpose of this litigation. We don't believe that X, Y, and Z is the case. We believe it's something else. Then we need reference material. We need documents that were produced at the same time, that is, the same period, time-period. We need documents that were produced from the same office, if it's an office document or at home. We need paperwork that we can tie down to see if that piece of paper was in use by that author at the time. I would ESDA the letter. Sorry to mention that word again, but I would ESDA the letter so see if there are any indentations that would give some hint as to something wrong with the chronology or those sort of things. Examining a document, as it were, in isolation, is extremely difficult. If there was physical damage to the document and alterations had be made and, as you have said, if the date of birth had been changed in pen from one to the other, that's happened, but we can't say anything else about it. And it is for this reason that I asked for permission to examine all of the diaries, because that is my reference material. Only a given few diaries were of any relevance to those instructing me, but only by examining all of the diaries can I see if there are any habits, any recurring faults, and things like this. And basically the only habit that -- apart from the smoothness of the writing and the neatness is the business of tearing a page out whenever -- for whatever reason. It doesn't appear to be a page that was written on, so it's possibly before the writing got there. And that happens book after book after book. But without that reference material, and examining only the few books on which I was instructed, I would have nothing to base anything. All of the anomalies I have found would remain totally unexplained. That's why I needed to examine all the other books. I have a wealth of examination reference material in those other books.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it be true that over the course of your employment with the UK immigration services the bulk of your work involved the assessment of identification-related documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Um, not altogether true, no. It's -- certainly I examined thousands of passports when I was on the desk, but when I moved to the specialist unit in 1983, I had to examine all manner of documents. Because once you move into the specialist unit, you're working for more than just the port you're working at. You're working for police, customs, other government agencies. And you're examining all manner of documents. And then they're not necessarily documents of identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could I ask you, then, if it's not the bulk, could you give us a percentage, what approximately was the percentage of passports and driving licences? Was that up to 88 per cent, approximately? I am not asking you -- or was it 40 per cent, or was it 60 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What, documents of identity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- as compared with the rest?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 60/40, I would have thought. As a guess only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because there were a great many other. I mean, I examined bank notes and bank cheques and things of that nature as well, not documents of identity, but they were in possession of passengers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you would say that approximately 40 per cent was outside the realm of the identity documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On page 1 of your report you summarise your understanding of the instructions related to your examination of the Mladic notebooks and the Jankovic diary. You say, in the first paragraph of this section: "The handwriting, all in Cyrillic script, has been forensically examined and I have been instructed that it is accepted that Mladic wrote all of the books. I have no difficulty in accepting that assertion."

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: What page? I beg your pardon, what paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's on page 1 of your report. Let me see if I can assist you with the paragraph number. It's directly under "2 instructions." There's no paragraph number.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yeah, I see that. I do apologise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There is no dispute that the handwriting in the notebooks purported to be that of Mladic is in fact his handwriting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Well, I -- I -- I understand that the report written by - and I do beg your pardon, again, Kerzan - Dr. Kerzan has been accepted. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you accept that it is Mladic's handwriting with respect to all of the notebooks you examined. You saw nothing in your examination that made you think, "Wait a minute, this may be of a different person"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I didn't. Because I had been, A, instructed that the case I've gone through, Dr. Kerzan's report, and noted that he used exactly the same methods when compare handwriting that I would use, but obviously he understands Cyrillic, I don't. I can see nothing to fault his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this is true even with respect to books in which you found anomalies, whether they be loose pages that were inserted, damaged books, misaligned pages - all of the writing on the pages is Mladic's?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I have some problems with this question, and I'll explain to you why. It appears to me that the testimony of the witness is: I saw a report in which the handwriting is analysed as to the author.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In that report I didn't find anything that surprised me. It methodologically is the type of report we would have produced ourselves, and I didn't pay any attention to authorship any further. Now, if you ask him if on the books in which anomalies were found, whether the witness saw anything which would cast doubt on the authorship, the first question would be, is whether the anomalies he found have triggered a change in approach, a change in attitude, so as to deviate from the general approach which is: I'm not looking at authorship matters. That's the first question to be put. And only if that question has been answered in the affirmative, I think then your question would be an appropriate question. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to jump to my feet as well because we would ask the Prosecution to clarify their case, because they have called evidence through Milovanovic which puts this issue slightly more ambiguously concerning the writing in the diary. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if the witness has not looked at it, he could not even give contradictory evidence to the Prosecution case because he has no evidence on that. That's the first thing I want to establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I agree with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only after that we may come - I'm not saying we'll come - but we may come to a question as you raised. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We would like -- I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But we would like the Prosecution to clarify that is some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's another matter. But I would first like to focus on that first question. Mr. Groome, in order to give any weight to nonobservance of any anomalies in terms of authorship, we should first ask the witness whether, on those books where he found anomalies of another kind, whether that changed his attitude, whether it changed his approach to further look into authorship matters as dealt with in the other report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept that that should be the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, Mr. Browne, I take it that you've heard the question. So rather than we repeat it, can I ask you to answer Judge Orie's question.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I didn't examine the handwriting for authorship. I'm not able to examine the handwriting for authorship. And I just didn't touch that part of the -- the case, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even not in the books where you found anomalies of another kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not something I could undertake. I am not familiar with handwriting in Cyrillic. I am not familiar with Serbian -- the Serbian language. It would have -- I would have been unable to do it in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you didn't notice anything where you suddenly thought that, Although I can't give an opinion about it, it nevertheless surprises me that suddenly everything is double the size or -- of handwriting. I mean --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, frankly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- because it wasn't there for me to look at in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But even if you feel incompetent to carefully study and draw conclusions and nevertheless something jumps into your eye, and that didn't even happen in this respect on the books in which you find anomalies of a different character?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. The problem with examining things under the infrared and ultraviolet lights, we're look at minutiae. And I'm looking at a differently aspect, as it were. And the matter of the handwriting is for other people, not for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And therefore, that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's unequivocal: You did not undertake any examination of any handwriting in any of these books?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Not in the terms of forgery and that sort of thing. Of course, I could look at a page in the round and say that's all very neatly written, but I don't know what is written or, indeed, whose written it, and it's -- that was none of my business, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I guess this is what I'm trying to work out: So it seems you did do some examination of the handwriting. You examined it for neatness or sloppiness, as it might be, but you did no examination with respect to authorship?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: That is correct. I mean, it was just -- this is all very neatly written, there are very few alterations, there are -- that is something that is just observational. It does not impinge on or indeed require forensic examination of the handwriting to see who wrote any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I could return to Judge Orie's question to you: When you found a page that was misaligned or was loose and inserted, did you pay particular attention to whether that page was neater or less neat than the other pages in the book?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Not particularly. What I was more interested in was seeing whether the inks had changed between the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we bring to our screens 65 ter 6436, and this is the handwriting analysis report prepared for the Seselj case by document examiner Dorijan Kerzan. And when you can see it on your screen, I would just ask you to confirm whether this is the report that you had access to and that you accepted and relied upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we could perhaps move to the next page, I think, is where we actually see -- I apologise. One more page. There we go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we go to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that's what I have before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 6436.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6436 will receive number P3109, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, it appears from your report and your evidence here today that the methodology that you used in examining each notebook included its examination under the VSC 6000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I think you characterise that machine as being a sophisticated piece of scientific equipment.

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And among the several tests that you can do, it seems that you have mentioned that you can examine documents under infrared light, ultraviolet light, and oblique light; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Effectively, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And am I correct in my understanding of this piece equipment -- piece of -- this piece of equipment, that it replaces several older pieces of separate equipment?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes. The basic premises -- premise was, I think, when Foster and Freeman designed it, that they would try and combine as many methods as they could into the one machine and the findings would go straight to computer, and so on. It enables the taking of enlargements and things of that nature as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it -- and in addition to it being more convenient for the examiner, it would also reduce the amount of wear and tear, as it were, in moving a document or book from machine to machine; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a fair comment. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was it in full working order during your examination, or at least the features that you attempted to use?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: As I understand it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you have any difficulty using the machine?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I wasn't -- I didn't use it. It was part of the protocol that the NFI expert manipulated the machine, control it, and opened it and closed the door, and so on and so forth. But when I -- you know, when I needed something taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were they able to do everything that you requested them to do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: As far as I understand, yes, I got results.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you look at every page of every notebook under both infrared and ultraviolet light?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: No. Only when I -- I certainly went through every page of the notebooks to compare the ultraviolet light, yes. And the infrared light I didn't, unless I found an anomaly that would attract my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what kind of anomaly attracted your attention and made you decide to request infrared light?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: If we -- if I found that there'd been a change in the paper reaction to ultraviolet, then I would check that the infrared characteristics of the writing across from one page to the other page were -- were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't quite understand that. Am I -- do I -- are you saying that if you had suspicions about whether the pages, the adjacent pages, were really in fact from the same book, you would use that feature to give you more information about the inks in the paper?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes. If there was a sudden change in the ultraviolet light - I've lost the word, I do beg your pardon - features, if you like, or reaction, from one page to another, it could be purely accidental, because in that particular book - and I think I explained it earlier, Your Honour. When we have the sewn books, whether a section had come from just a different paper run, rather than evidence of fraud, I would still look at the infrared characteristics of the inks to make sure that we hadn't got ink A with that particular infrared finding and then suddenly we got the paper of a different chemical recipe and ink B is a completely different pen. That would be, in my view, anomalous and would require a great deal more looking at. But if I found that the paper had changed but the ink hadn't and the writing hadn't, and as far as one could see, as far as neatness and so on and so forth, then I wouldn't have bothered beyond checking the ink for infrared characteristics and then carried on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in preparation to examine you, I looked through the manual of the VSC 6000. And is my understanding correct that it has the capacity to take photographs under whatever feature you're using, whether it's the microscope, the infrared light, whatever lighting feature you're using, it has the capacity to document what you're seeing?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you in fact take pictures of some of your observations?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: I took a great many.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And none of the pictures or photographs made it into the report. Can you explain? Was there nothing remarkable about the photographs? Would they not have assisted us in understanding your finding?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: They would have done if we'd had the books in court, but we hadn't. And the -- the -- the photographs do not necessarily help in illustration, in isolation. I -- all the photographs are available if anybody wants to look at them, but they don't actually mean a great deal unless you've got something to point to, and we haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you -- you gave evidence earlier today that in the middle of a meeting it seemed that the ink of the pen was changed. Would we have been able to see that, or would we be able to see it, on the photograph of that page if you had taken such a photograph?

utterances.speaker: DAVID BROWNE
utterances.text: If you're -- let's see, infrared light will -- if you have a book or a page that is written all in black ink, infrared light would be able to identify whether all of that black ink was in the same chemical recipe as rest of the page. If you have black ink and you change to blue ink, then it's an irrelevance, because infrared characteristics may alter, they may be exactly the same, and yet we can see it's black ink and blue ink. There is no probative value in that -- in doing that test. It's only when you get difference within the same colour. And we went to great trouble in the NFI. In some cases, at first glance, you'd think, Well, that looks different ink. Shall we get excited? And by the time we had put the VSC to work - and it really is an excellent piece of kit - by the time we had put the VSC to work, we were able to establish that, no, it wasn't. It wasn't a different ink at all, it was exactly the same, and we can forget about it. Because it wasn't an anomaly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think it's the appropriate time to conclude for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Browne -- I'm looking at Mr. Groome. Mr. Groome, how much time do you think you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's difficult to estimate at this juncture, Your Honour. Could I please maybe advise the Chamber in the morning? I'll take a look at my notes and I'll find out how much time I've used so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well I'm not interested in whether it's 40 or 45 minutes, but I'm interested in whether it's one hour and a half or -- I think your indication was two hours and a half to start with. Has that changed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour. I think I'll be within that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there's a fair expectation that we could end either at the end of the first session or somewhere in the beginning of the second session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think that's reasonable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would that -- Mr. Browne, I'm exploring with the parties how long we keep you hosted here. Mr. Jordash, as matters stand now, would you expect --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 to 20 minutes. Mr. Petrovic, you're still --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not expect that I shall need any time as matters stand now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Browne, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. And I instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony already given today or whether it's testimony still to be given tomorrow. And as you may have noticed from the answers, that there is a fair chance, and that's the weak expression, that we'll conclude your testimony somewhere tomorrow morning. We stand adjourned. And we resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 21st of March, Courtroom II, 9.00 in the morning.
